final:
**The Drowned Birch Wood**

A flooded birch grove at evening: two dark birch trunks cut by the left edge of the frame, a broad sky glazed with warm cloud bands over a cool blue, a luminous band of vapour lying on the far water where a stand of pale birches stands with its reflections running toward the viewer, and open, quiet water with a small boat and two mooring stakes. In the foreground a low bank carries a fallen birch, and a woman in a dark coat stands at the water's edge with her back to us, looking out at the mist.

It is painted the way his notes describe his method — a warm ground under a lead-white top on fine linen, a precise pencil drawing, one very thin underpainting, and then thin layers whose gradations come from glazing and stippling rather than from thick blending, so the weave and the drawing still show through. The work took fourteen days on the painting's own clock; the long struggle was the middle distance, where each veil of mist that softened the wood also half buried it.

**Flooded Birch Wood (Evening)** — 297 chunks, on the linen easel.

The picture is a drowned wood at dusk: two dark birches cut by the left edge close the view, a broad evening sky glazed with cream and blue-grey cloud bands, a luminous band of vapour lying along the far shore, and a stand of pale birches standing in still water with a breath of reflection under each of them. Open water fills the middle, with a soft swell or two and a path of reflected light; at the bottom a dark near bank runs along with a fallen birch, and on it a woman in a shawl stands at the water's edge, seen from behind.

I spent the second half of the work taking the picture apart and putting it back together: the reflections had been painted as white candles, the near trunks were barred like ladders where the sky showed through the gaps, and the water was a woolly mess of over-painted glazes. What finally worked was to decide each passage's value once and lay the whole middle down in order — the water flat and opaque, then the wood, then the reflections — and to touch nothing over it afterwards. The journal has the rest of it: a wandering hand on a fine brush, tapered marks that read as needles and leaves, the blender dragging the black off the trunks into the sky, and the one rule I had already written down on day 7 and still had to learn a third time.

final:
I've stopped. The painting is **_Flooded Birch Wood (Evening)_**.

The picture is a flooded birch wood at evening. Two dark birches are cut by the left edge, their bare branches crossing a broad sky laid in grey and cream cloud bands, with the last warmth along the horizon. A band of vapour lies on the far water — the lightest passage in the picture — and a stand of bare birches stands in the flood, their tops drawn back into that vapour and their reflections running down beneath them. Open water carries a dozen drawn ripples, and a dark near bank runs along the bottom with a fallen birch lying on it, a few tufts and pebbles, and a small figure in a dark coat standing at the water's edge, seen from behind.

I inherited the composition and threw away most of the paint. What I kept was the idea and the bones; what I rebuilt was the value structure, the wood, the water and the light. The session cost180 chunks and taught me more than the first nineteen days had — chiefly that coverage is not film (three passes bury what one never will, and only opaque pigment buries anything), that painting onto tacky paint mixes rather than covers, and that a narrow patch leaves a ridge which comes back as the surface dries. My journal had all three of those lessons written down already; I had to lose the sky to each of them twice before they actually stuck.

final:
**Flooded Birch Wood, Evening**

The picture is a drowned birch wood at last light. Two dark birches are cut by the left edge, their bare limbs reaching into a grey evening sky that still carries the last of the cloud. A wide band of luminous vapour lies along the far shore with a dark wood standing behind it, and in front of that, the wood itself — a stand of bare birches standing in the flood in three ranks, dark in front and pale behind, their reflections running straight down into still water. The flood is open, with a swell or two, a drowned branch and a clump of reeds at the right; then a near bank with a fallen birch along it, tufts of grass, and a small figure standing at the water's edge, seen from behind.

The value range runs from about fifteen in the near trunks to about ninety in the vapour, with the dark band of the far wood between them — the thing my earlier notes said three sessions running that the picture lacked.
